title: Nobody here is verified
body: The ladder on a profile states four facts and nothing more: an email was confirmed, a parcel from this shop was delivered, a number of outings were completed on this board, and a number of people who actually walked with them said so. None of that is an identity check. DEWDROPZ does not verify who anyone is, how fit they are, or whether they can lead. Read the badges as facts about an account, not as a character reference.

title: The meeting point is held back on purpose
body: You see the general area when you request. The exact point is released only once three people are going, counting the host, and four for camping and stargazing. That is a database rule, not a UI nicety, and it exists so nobody ever meets one stranger alone at a road head. A host who offers to send you the point early is handing away the safeguard.

title: Everything stays on the plan's page
body: No phone numbers, no Instagram, no dm me. There is no messaging here and that is deliberate: the moment arrangements move off the page, nothing about who said what is on the record. Every free-text box is scanned and a number is refused outright, so if a post of yours was blocked, this is why. If somebody asks you to take it elsewhere, report them instead of answering.

title: What to dial, and where help arrives
body: 112 for anything, 108 for an ambulance. Save both before you leave, along with the forest chowki or SDRF post nearest the road head if the plan names one. Help does not come up the hill to you, it arrives at the road head, so somebody has to walk down or reach signal. Decide at the start who does that if it goes wrong.

title: Shared jeeps go when they are full
body: Nothing out of Dehradun ISBT or the Mussoorie taxi stand runs to a timetable. A Sumo leaves when 8 or 9 seats are taken. At 6 am that can be 20 minutes. By afternoon it can be two hours, or the price of the whole vehicle. Work backwards from how the sharing fills, not from the drive time your phone shows.

title: Sort the way down before you go up
body: Ask your driver on the way up when he makes his last run down, and treat that hour as your turn-around time. It varies by road, by season and by how many people are about, so ask rather than assume. Carry the fare in 50s and 100s. UPI stops working somewhere above the bazaar and nobody has change for a 500.

title: Difficulty here means the climb
body: The board has three words, easy, moderate and difficult, and most hosts pick one by how the day felt to them. Read the height gain instead. Under 400 m of gain is easy, 400 to 800 m is a moderate day, over 800 m is a difficult one whatever the distance says. 6 km with 900 m of gain is a hard day. If the host has not written the gain, ask on the page before you request.

title: A ridge is not a flat walk
body: Ridge routes in Garhwal roll. You gain and lose 100 m a dozen times and the total is far more than the distance suggests. There is usually no water on top, no shade, and the wind does not stop. Carry the full 3 litres and a windproof for a ridge day even when the profile looks easy.

title: Agree the sweep and the turn time before you leave
body: When cloud comes in or a knee goes, the group splits. The quick three pull ahead and the slowest person ends up alone at the back in the worst of it. Settle at the meeting point who walks last and what time everyone turns, whatever the top is doing. Make that call while people are still dry, because once they are wet and cold they will argue for pushing on. If it splits anyway, go down with whoever is heading for the road head.

title: The way down is where people get hurt
body: Below about 2,000 m it is chir pine needles, which roll under a sole like ball bearings. Above that it is oak litter and mud, which is worse after rain and is what people slip on coming off Nag Tibba. Tired legs stop lifting your feet properly. Go down slower than feels reasonable, take shorter steps, and if there is one pole in the group give it to whoever is struggling.

title: Signal follows the ridge, not the map
body: You will have full bars on a spur and nothing in the valley 200 m below it, and the camp is almost always in the dead patch while the top is fine. No network holds everywhere in these hills, whatever anyone tells you about their SIM. Send your starting-now message from the road head and assume the next one goes out only when you climb back into the open. Chasing signal all day is how you reach dusk with a flat phone.

title: February to mid-June is fire season
body: The chir belt below Mussoorie and around Rishikesh burns every spring, worst in April and May. It shows as smoke sitting in the valley all day, ground litter still smouldering beside the path, and forest roads shut without notice. Check before you drive out. Do not walk through burning ground to save time, and expect that a plan may be called off at the road head in those weeks.

title: Elephants and leopards
body: Rishikesh-side trails run through and beside Rajaji. Wild elephants use the forest roads at dawn and dusk and they kill people in Uttarakhand every year. If you meet one, go back the way you came and do not try to pass. Leopards on the Dehradun and Mussoorie fringe are the concrete reason nobody drops far behind near dusk. Keep the group closed up in the first and last hour of light.

title: Jonk are a monsoon fact, not a cancellation
body: The monsoon breaks here in the last week of June, not in July. From then until September the wet forest below about 2,000 m, the Rishikesh side and the lower approaches to Nag Tibba, is jonk country. The bite does not hurt and land leeches carry nothing, but it bleeds for an hour and the site gets infected if you scratch it open. Odomos or any DEET repellent on socks and boot uppers works better than tucking trousers in, which they simply climb over.

title: The nala you crossed in the morning
body: A dry stream bed can be thigh deep two hours after a storm on a slope you cannot even see. Do not cross a nala in spate. Wait it out or turn back, they drop as fast as they rise. On the Rishikesh side the same rule covers the river: the Ganga's current is nothing like it looks from the bank, and the pools above the waterfalls are where the drownings actually happen.

title: Treat the water
body: Do not count on a spring being where somebody said it was, and do not count on the Maggi point being open out of season. Carry 2 to 3 litres. If you are refilling from a stream on an overnight or a multi-day trip, boil it, use tablets or carry a filter. There is more grazing and there are more villages above these catchments than you would guess.

title: Altitude starts higher than people think
body: AMS is uncommon below 2,500 m and almost everything around Mussoorie sits under that. Nag Tibba's top is 3,022 m and the usual trip sleeps at base camp around 2,500 m, so a headache there is far more likely to be dehydration, sun or a skipped meal. The real threshold is Kedarkantha at 3,810 m and the passes beyond Sankri. Above 3,000 m expect a headache and a bad night, drink more than you feel like, and if the headache worsens as you climb, the only fix is going down.

title: Low is not the same as safe
body: Nothing around Mussoorie is high enough for altitude to hurt you. What hurts people at these heights is a slip on a wet descent, a nala in spate, a road accident on the ghat, and being caught out after dark. Do not read only 2,000 m as easy day.

title: Daylight, and the torch nobody packs
body: In late December it is not properly light in Dehradun until about 07:00 and it is dark by about 17:30. In June you have roughly three more usable hours across the day. A 5 am start in January is two hours of walking in the dark, and a December turn-around has to be hours earlier than a June one. Carry a headtorch on every outing, including the ones you are certain will be back by lunch.

title: Photographs
body: Ask before you photograph someone and ask again before you post or tag them. Plenty of people here have not told their family they are out with strangers, and some have good reasons for not being findable. If someone says no, that is the end of it. If a photo of you goes up and you want it down, ask once and report it if it stays.

title: Drink is where these go wrong
body: Alcohol on a camping or stargazing plan changes who can drive, who can find the tents, and who is able to help if somebody is hurt. If a plan involves drinking, the host should say so on the page so nobody arrives expecting something else. Whoever is driving is not drinking, and that is decided before you leave, not at midnight in a car park.

title: If it collapses at the road head
body: The host does not show, or two people drop out and it is you and one stranger. That is exactly what the meeting-point floor exists to prevent, so treat it the same way: do not go on as a pair with somebody you have never met. Go home. It costs you a fare and a morning. Then report the no-show so it is on the record.

title: Women-only is enforced by the database
body: A women-only trip is not a label a host is trusted to honour. The join is refused outright at the database, and a man cannot post one either, so the host is a woman too. Your gender is asked once, used only for this gate, never shown on your profile and never filterable by anyone. Filter the board to women-only whenever you want the question off the table entirely.

title: Reading a host
body: A good host writes the dull things in advance: height gain, back-by time, how everyone gets home, how many are confirmed. The one to skip keeps it vague or says it will be sorted out there. Watch for a trip cancelled and reposted again and again, because the date, hour and place are frozen once a plan goes up, so repeated reposts mean something is being moved around. The one thing a decent host never does is ask you to arrange anything off this page. That is not a judgement call, it is a report.

title: Look at who is already confirmed
body: Before you request, read the roster and the profiles on it. Count the walks, the vouches, and how long the accounts have existed. If everyone going is a new account with nothing behind it and no other woman is confirmed, wait for a different plan. You can ask the host on the page how many women are confirmed, and if the host will not answer that, do not go.

title: Travel out with somebody
body: Arriving with a friend, or with another woman off the same plan, changes the whole day. You get a second read on the group and a simple reason to leave when you want one. Do not post your neighbourhood on the page to arrange it. Your profile already carries your home town and the board lets people find others setting off from the same place. Ask the host to introduce two confirmed people to each other instead.

title: Have your own way home before you go
body: Work it out that morning: which vehicle, from where, until what time, and the cash for it. Then say it flatly and early, before anybody offers you a lift. I am going back on the 4 o'clock share is a complete answer and needs no reason attached. A good host has already written this on the page.

title: Toilets
body: There is nothing past the last dhaba, and on an open ridge there is no cover either. Drinking less to dodge the problem is the real mistake, and a lot of the headaches people blame on altitude start there. Go at the last shop. On the trail, say out loud that you are stopping, step off the path where you can still see the group, and carry the tissue out in a bag. Do not go far out of sight for privacy, because loose ground with nobody watching is how a turned ankle becomes a rescue.

title: Write the numbers, not the mood
body: Height gain in metres, distance, back-by time, how people get home, and what you will do if the weather turns. Moderate, easy-going vibe tells a stranger nothing, and it is how you end up with somebody on the hill who cannot finish. The dull version fills faster than the friendly one because it lets people judge themselves out.

title: Declining costs you nothing
body: You decide who comes and you owe nobody a reason. A decline reveals nothing to the person declined. If the request reads wrong, if the intro is empty, if somebody is arguing about the pace before they have even joined, decline it. Saying no to a stranger now is easier than managing them at 2,000 m with four other people waiting.

title: The meeting-point floor is yours too
body: Three people going for a day outing, four for camping and stargazing, before the exact point is released. Do not work around it. No early reveal to one person, no I will tell you where when you get here. The floor exists so that nobody, you included, ends up meeting one stranger alone. If a plan is not filling, cancel it or accept that it does not run.

title: You cannot edit the time or the place
body: Once a plan is up, the date, hour, activity and meeting area are fixed. Changing any of them means cancelling and posting again, and everyone confirmed is told the old one is off. So get them right before you post. Cancelling and reposting the same trip repeatedly reads badly to anyone paying attention, and it should.

title: No-shows and last-minute drops
body: Write on the page how long you will wait at the meeting point, say 15 minutes, so nobody argues about it on the day. If someone confirmed does not turn up and does not say why, remove them from the roster so it is on their record. If you have to call it off, cancel on the board rather than going quiet, because a cancellation reaches everyone confirmed and silence reaches nobody.

title: Say who is coming back with whom
body: Before you set off, out loud and as a roll call: who walks sweep, what time everyone turns, and how each person gets home. That is the whole of what a host is responsible for out there. Not leading, not deciding for grown adults, just making sure nobody's way back is an assumption.

title: The day starts the night before
body: A 6 am meet in Dehradun means being up around 04:30, and the drive is longer than people say. Roughly 1 to 1.5 hours to the Mussoorie trail heads, 3.5 to 4 to Pantwari for Nag Tibba, 9 to 10 to Sankri. Read the plan for which one it is. Eat something small before the drive, and if ghat roads turn your stomach stay off your phone, because the front seat in a shared jeep is usually sold already.

title: You will be slower than the plan says
body: Uphill on a rough path with a day pack, most people manage about 2 km an hour, not the 4 they walk on the flat. A 6 km climb is most of a morning. That is normal and it is not a verdict on your fitness. Say your real pace at the meeting point so the group plans around it instead of discovering it at noon.

title: Shoes decide the day
body: Grip matters more than brand, and having already worn them in matters more than either. Smooth-soled sneakers on dry pine needles are how people go down hard on the way back. The moment you feel a hot spot on your heel, stop and tape it there, not at the next halt. A blister at kilometre 2 slows the whole group, not only you.

title: You get cold ten minutes after being hot
body: You climb soaked in sweat, then stand still on a ridge in the wind, and wet cotton stays wet. Carry a windproof layer and put it on when you stop, before you feel cold rather than after. A dry t-shirt at the bottom of the bag, worn only at the top, is the cheapest comfort you can carry.

title: Carry your own food and water
body: 2 to 3 litres, and your own food. The Maggi point at the top exists on some trails and is shut on the rest, especially out of season. Eat before you are hungry and keep something sweet for the way down, because that is when the crash comes. Tired plus hungry is when people fall.

title: Ask on the page before you request
body: Height gain, pace, how people are getting there and back, whether there is anywhere to refill water. Asking is free and it is not rude, and a host would far rather answer four questions now than deal with a surprise on the hill. The one thing not to ask for is a phone number or a handle. Everything happens on the page.

title: Getting home at 2 am is the dangerous part
body: A stargazing plan can run to 02:00, and the board will not accept the post until the host has written down how everyone gets back. Read that line before you request. The shared vehicles stopped hours ago, so somebody is driving a ghat road in the dark at the end of a long day, and that drive is more likely to hurt you than anything on the hill. Ask who is driving, whether they have slept, and how many are in the car.

title: It is colder than the forecast
body: You are standing still for three hours with no sun, and a ridge at midnight is nothing like the Dehradun number on your phone. Bring more layers than feels sensible, something to sit on, and gloves from October onward. Bring a headtorch with a red mode, because one white beam wipes out everyone's dark adaptation for 20 minutes.

title: Pitching in the dark
body: Camping plans can start as late as 19:00, which means walking in and pitching after dark. Get the tents up and the water sorted before anything else. Fix in your head where camp sits relative to the path while there is still light, because a camp is easy to walk away from at night and very hard to find on the way back.

title: Who sleeps where, agreed in daylight
body: Ask before you request: how many tents, who is sharing with whom, and whether there is a homestay or a room option. Get the answer on the page in writing, not at 22:00 at the campsite. Carrying your own tent removes the question completely and is worth the weight. A women-only camping plan removes it too, and that one is enforced by the database rather than trusted to anybody.

title: A multi-day trip is a different decision
body: The board takes trips up to a month long, and day 4 is nothing like a Sunday walk with the same people. You cannot leave when you feel like it, the group is the only group there is, and a bad fit on day one is a bad fit for a week. Ask who has done this route, what happens if somebody has to go down, and who is carrying the first-aid kit. Walk with the host on a day outing before you commit to a week with them.

title: Permits, entry fees and insurance
body: Sankri sits inside Govind Pashu Vihar, with a forest entry fee and paperwork. Nanda Devi, the Valley of Flowers and the inner-line areas each have their own rules, and anything outside Uttarakhand adds visas and permits on top. Ask the host who is arranging them and what your share costs before you commit. Trekking insurance that actually covers evacuation is not standard and nobody will remind you to buy it.

title: Go up slowly enough
body: On anything crossing 3,000 m the schedule matters more than your fitness. Climb high and sleep low where the route allows, and treat a rest day as part of the plan rather than a wasted one. If somebody has a headache that worsens as you climb, is unsteady on their feet, or is breathless at rest, the answer is to go down that day. No drug makes going up higher safe.

title: Ghat descents and trucks
body: The run down from Mussoorie is about 30 km of blind hairpins shared with buses and trucks that will not see you. Ride single file, take the outside line only where you can see through the bend, and check your brakes at the top rather than halfway down. Lights on in daylight. In fire season and after rain there is loose gravel and ash sitting on the apex of every bend.

title: A run splits the group by design
body: A running plan spreads over kilometres inside the first 20 minutes, so the usual advice about staying together does not apply and something else has to take its place. Agree the exact route, the turn-around point and where everyone waits, before you start. Nobody runs the last section alone in the dark. Carry water even on a 10 km loop, because nothing here is flat and there are no taps.

title: The 4:30 start is the point
body: The birds are up before you and quiet by 09:00, so these plans start in the dark and the walk in is by torch. It is slow standing about in the cold rather than a workout, so bring more layers than a trek would need. Keep voices down and phones on silent. The group behind you is why the group in front stopped seeing anything.

title: Post the hour you leave the city, not the hour you start walking
body: Mussoorie is 35 km and an hour and a bit. Pantwari, the roadhead for Nag Tibba, is about 90 km and three hours of hill road. Same board, very different days — a five-hour walk from Pantwari is a twelve-hour day door to door. Put the departure hour and the roadhead in the plan. Shared jeeps back from the roadheads thin out through the afternoon and then stop.

title: Fix a turnaround time, and carry a torch whatever the plan says
body: In late December the sun is down in Dehradun by about 17:25, and under oak or chir you are on a torch from 17:00. A party planning to be back by six is planning to walk in the dark. Decide the hour you turn round before you start, and turn then even if the top looks twenty minutes away. From April onward the cloud builds after midday, so being off an open ridge by two is the plan, not the fallback.

title: People get hurt going down
body: The descent is where it happens: tired legs on a surface that moves. Chir needles over dust on the lower Doon slopes, wet oak leaf litter and greasy limestone higher up. Budget two-thirds of your ascent time for the way down, not half. A stick picked up at the roadhead costs nothing and takes real load off the knees.

title: Mid-June to mid-September the road is the problem
body: The monsoon closes roads, drops slopes onto them, and fills nalas that were dry in the morning. A crossing you walked through at ten can be impassable at four, and the answer is to wait or turn back, never to link arms and try it. Leeches on the Thano and Rishikesh side. If you post in this season, say in the plan what happens if the road is blocked on the way out.

title: The dawn rule is for forest, not for Asan in winter
body: Forest birds call from first light and are largely done ninety minutes later, so a Maldevta morning — 12 to 15 km out, half an hour — means leaving Dehradun in the dark. Asan is a wetland, and from November to March the wintering ducks sit there all day. Benog is beyond Mussoorie, closer to two hours. Match the hour to the site rather than to a rule.

title: Asan and Benog have gates, tickets and an opening hour
body: Both are protected areas with an entry fee and a barrier that opens when it opens. You cannot be inside before first light because you set a 05:00 alarm. Check the current gate hour and fee before you post a start time, or the group stands at a barrier in the dark having driven an hour. Open ground like Maldevta and the canal roads has no such gate.

title: Single file, phones silent, no playback
body: Sound carries in these valleys, and six people talking clear a slope well before anyone sees anything. Walk in a line with gaps, one person setting the pace at the front, hand signals agreed before you set off. Do not play calls off a phone — around Benog it pushes pheasants off territory, and it marks you with the people who know the ground. One pair of binoculars between five means four bored people, so the plan should say who is bringing what.

title: Say road or trail, with the climb in metres
body: Two different sports under one word. Dehradun to Mussoorie is roughly 33 km and about 1,400 m of ascent on a live highway. The Maldevta and Sahastradhara-side tracks are loose, steep and no place for a road bike. Put the surface, the distance and the metres of climb in the plan, and say what happens to whoever gets dropped — there is no way to phone them once the group is strung out over a hill.

title: Keep left, and expect the danger to be coming down at you
body: Tourist taxis and buses cut across the crown of the road on blind hairpins, and weekends and the summer season are worse. Ride single file and hold the left, but off the very edge, where gravel and rockfall sit after rain. Never overtake anything on the outside of a bend. Be past Rajpur by first light and off the road before the traffic builds mid-morning — do not invent a start so early that you are climbing unlit among night trucks.

title: The descent is a braking problem, not a pedalling one
body: Mussoorie down to Rajpur is twenty-odd kilometres of continuous braking. Light constant drag is what cooks a rim and boils fluid: brake firm and intermittent, alternate front and rear, and stop to let everything cool. It is around ten degrees warmer at the bottom, so the layer goes on at the top, not at Rajpur. Tube, levers, pump, and knowing how to use them — the nearest shop is down in the valley.

title: The climb takes the minute, not the altitude
body: At 2,000 m a 5:30 runner loses seconds a kilometre to the thin air, not a minute. What takes the minute is the gradient and the surface — loose stone, roots, steps. Read a plan's metres of ascent before its distance. Ten kilometres with 600 m of climb is not a ten-kilometre run, and pacing it like one is how you end up walking the last third.

title: Post the pace you will actually run and the pace you will wait for
body: The vertical decides the pace here, so ten kilometres easy tells nobody anything. State the pace per kilometre, the metres of ascent, and the slowest pace you will hold at junctions. A run advertised at a pace nobody holds ends with two people missing on an unfamiliar forest track and no way to call them.

title: Dogs are the daily hazard on the Rajpur and Maldevta tracks
body: Dog packs around the villages and the fringe come at runners far more often than anything else does. Stop running, walk, face them, keep something in your hand and something between you and them. Leopards use the same forest tracks at first and last light, which is why a six o'clock start belongs on open track and why nobody runs those tracks alone at dusk.

title: Dress for three hours of standing still
body: Standing still at 2,000 m is a different cold from any walk. On the Mussoorie ridge in December it is near freezing before you add wind. Fleece and windproof, cap, gloves, and something to sit or lie on so the ground is not taking your heat. The usual failure is one person underdressed, cold by half ten, and the whole group driving home early. A flask of chai does more than any equipment.

title: Check the moon, and know which season you are asking for
body: Within three or four days of full there is nothing to see but the moon. October to December is the clearest, driest air here — winter sky, Orion, the Pleiades, and no Milky Way core. The core sits low in the south, straight over the Doon's light dome: in April and May you get it in the small hours, and by the time it is up in the evening it is July, and July is cloud. Get behind the ridge, away from the valley.

title: The drive home at one in the morning is the actual risk
body: Standing in a field looking up is not dangerous. Thirty kilometres of hairpins at 01:00, awake since six, is. The board will not take a stargazing plan that does not say how everyone gets back in the dark, so write who is driving and whether that person has slept. If there is no good answer, it is a plan for another night. Red light only once you are there — one white beam costs everybody twenty minutes of night vision.

title: Where you may actually pitch, and where you may not
body: The riverside camps upstream of Rishikesh, on the Kaudiyala to Byasi stretch, were closed by the National Green Tribunal — old photographs are not permission. Rajaji is a national park and tiger reserve, shut to visitors from mid-June to mid-November, and public camping inside it is not a permission you apply for. That leaves registered sites and private land, mostly the Dhanaulti, Kanatal and Mussoorie belt. A fire in forest is an offence under the Forest Act; a bonfire at a licensed site is theirs to allow and not yours to assume. February to June the chir litter goes up like paper.

title: Carry the water in, and keep the food away from the tents
body: Assume the stream is dry or fouled — fill at the last village tap or carry a filter. Cook on gas. Wash and empty water sixty metres from any stream, and keep soap out of it entirely. Black bear are in the oak forest through the Nag Tibba and Dhanaulti belt, and macaques and dogs work every roadside site, so food goes in one bag away from where people sleep. Everything that went up comes back down, foil and scraps included.

title: A night out commits you in a way a day walk does not
body: You can turn back from a day walk at eleven in the morning. You cannot leave a ridge at eleven at night. Settle the sleeping arrangement in the plan itself before anyone travels — how many tents, who is in which, who carries what — because there is no messaging and the post cannot be edited later. Take the mat as seriously as the bag: at Dhanaulti and Kanatal, 2,200 to 2,500 m, a May night is around ten degrees, and at Nag Tibba it is single figures. If it runs more than one night, say what the water and food plan is for each.

title: Height gained per day is the whole safety plan
body: Above 3,000 m, sleep no more than 300 to 500 m higher than the night before and build in a day that does not climb. Headache, nausea or breathlessness at rest is altitude sickness, and descent is the only treatment that works — 500 m down, at night if it comes to that, and nobody walks down alone. Somebody being left to sleep off a bad headache higher up is the standard way this turns serious.

title: Kedarkantha in December is a snow trek, not the same walk
body: From December the snowline can sit below the last village and the summit day is a snow climb — microspikes, gaiters, boots stiff enough to take a spike, and a start early enough to be down before the afternoon softens it. The days are short and the cold at the campsites is the part people underestimate. The same route in October is a different trip and should not be posted as though it were the same one.

title: Rate a multi-day trek by its worst day, not its average
body: State the daily distance, the daily ascent, and where the group sleeps each night. Difficulty is set by the hardest day, the number of hard days back to back, the highest sleeping altitude, and whether there is a way off the hill part-way. Say in the plan what happens if one person has to turn back on day four. Who walks down with them is a decision made while posting, not at 4,000 m.

title: Past the roadhead there is no network, no ATM and no help
body: Govind Pashu Vihar takes an entry fee and a permit at Sankri. The last dependable ATM is back down at Purola or Mori, so carry cash for the whole trip and the jeep out. Signal ends at or before the roadhead. Leave your itinerary and the day you expect to be back in signal with someone at home, because nobody on this board can reach you and DEWDROPZ cannot either.

title: Everything has to go in the post, because nothing follows it
body: There is no messaging here, and a posted plan cannot be edited afterwards. So the things a group chat would normally settle — who brings the stove, who is driving, what the cab costs, who has the spare tube, how many tents — go in Getting there and Anything else at the moment you post. Whatever you leave out gets sorted at the meeting point or not at all.

title: Read the request, and decline without giving a reason
body: You are deciding who a group of strangers spends a day with, so read what the person wrote about themselves and about this particular walk. A request that says only that they are interested gives you nothing to act on. You can decline anyone, and you owe no explanation. If two people are borderline and the day is hard, take neither.

title: Anyone moving it off the board is a decline
body: There is no contact exchange here by design, so every arrangement stays on the walk's own page where it can be seen. If a request slips in a number, a handle or a UPI id, or asks for yours, decline it and report the person — Something else, with their exact words pasted into the box, because the queue only knows what you write there. The people who push at this rule are the people the rule is for.

title: Rate it for the slowest person you will accept
body: Moderate should mean somebody who walks most weekends finishes without help. Judge on ascent, distance and terrain together, and on the worst section rather than the average. Nag Tibba in a day is about 1,600 m of climb and is sold to beginners across the state — that does not make it an easy day. Say difficult and lose two people. Flatter it and you keep them, and bring one of them down in the dark at their pace.

title: Cancelling late is better than going
body: Weather, a nala in spate, a road that has gone, or your own condition are all reasons to call it off, and the honest time is the night before. Some of them you only learn on the morning, and it is still right to cancel then, at the meeting point, in front of everyone. People took leave for this. That thought is exactly how a host talks themselves into a day that should not have happened.

title: Name a back marker, and count at every junction
body: Somebody walks at the back, and the front does not go out of their sight. Junctions and rest stops are where people are lost, so count heads there, every time. If the group genuinely splits by pace, it splits into two groups that each know the route and the turnaround time, never into a fast group and whoever is left behind.

title: Women-only is enforced by the board, not by the note
body: A women-only walk can be posted only by a member whose profile says woman, and anyone else asking to join is refused where the row is written, not merely hidden in the interface. That answer is asked once, used only for this, never shown on your profile and not filterable by anyone. A plan that says women only in its text but is not marked women-only has none of that gate.

title: Nobody here needs your number
body: No one on this board has a reason to ask for your phone, your Instagram or your WhatsApp, and that includes the host. If someone asks, report them on their profile — Made me feel unsafe, or Something else, with what they wrote pasted in. You do not owe a reply first. Blocking is immediate and works both ways: they cannot see or join your walks either.

title: Know your way back before you accept a lift
body: The exact meeting point is held until three people are confirmed, four after dark, and it goes to the whole confirmed group rather than to one person. Meet the group there. Do not be collected alone from somewhere else beforehand, whatever the reason given. Work out before you go how you get home if the one car you were counting on leaves early — shared jeeps from the roadheads thin out through the afternoon and stop by evening.

title: What to put in Say hello
body: The host is choosing between strangers on three lines of text. Write your longest recent walk and roughly how long it took, the pace you are comfortable at, whether you are driving or need a seat, and anything that affects the group — a knee, asthma, no head for exposure. Leave out your number and your handle. A request with contact details in it is the easiest decline a host makes.

title: Read the ascent, not the rating
body: Easy, moderate and difficult are the host's opinion and nobody checks them. Metres of climb are a fact: 600 m of ascent over ten kilometres is a hard morning whatever the plan calls it. If a post states no ascent and no turnaround time, you are being asked to trust an estimate. There is no messaging, so you cannot ask — decide on what is written, and skip it if it does not say enough.

title: The list for any day walk in these hills
body: Two litres of water, a warm layer whatever the valley feels like, a torch even on a day walk, sun cover, cash because UPI does not work past the roadhead, and shoes you have already walked in. Blisters in the second hour are the most common way a day goes wrong. A charged phone is not a plan — signal here is patchy and gone at the roadheads.
